name: The Repugnant Conclusion
statement: Adding up welfare implies that a vast crowd of barely-worth-living lives can be better than a smaller world of flourishing ones.
statementAccent: a vast crowd of barely-worth-living lives can be better than a smaller world of flourishing ones
meaning: The repugnant conclusion is a problem in population ethics identified by the philosopher Derek Parfit in his 1984 book Reasons and Persons. Parfit stated it roughly as follows: for any possible population of at least ten billion people, all with a very high quality of life, there must be some much larger imaginable population whose existence, if other things are equal, would be better, even though its members have lives that are barely worth living. In other words, a smaller, flourishing population, call it A, can always be judged worse than a sufficiently enormous population, call it Z, each of whose members has a life only marginally above the point of not being worth living. Parfit found this conclusion deeply counterintuitive, indeed repugnant, and much of the work in population ethics has been an attempt to find a theory that avoids it while remaining consistent, an aim Parfit himself did not think he had achieved.
mechanism: The conclusion follows from total utilitarianism, or totalism, the view that the value of a population is the sum of the well-being of its members. If value is a total, then any loss in the quality of individual lives can in principle be compensated by a sufficient gain in the number of lives, so a huge population each with tiny but positive welfare will have a greater total than a smaller population with very high welfare, making Z better than A. Parfit reached the conclusion through the mere addition paradox, an argument using populations A, A plus, B minus, and B: adding extra people with lives worth worth living seems to make things no worse, a slightly larger population with more equal welfare seems better, and iterating these steps drives toward Z. Avoiding the conclusion by switching to average utilitarianism, which values mean well-being, generates its own counterintuitive results, and Parfit sought a Theory X that would escape all such problems. Later impossibility results, associated with Gustaf Arrhenius, argue that no population theory can satisfy every plausible condition at once.

examples.text: A flourishing population of ten billion is judged worse than an enormous population whose members' lives are barely worth living, because the total welfare is larger.
Parfit's step-by-step argument through populations A, A plus, B minus, and B leads, by seemingly innocent moves, toward the repugnant conclusion.
Parfit sought a Theory X avoiding the conclusion while blocking related paradoxes, but concluded he had not found one, and impossibility results suggest none may exist.

variants.name: Total versus average utilitarianism
variants.text: The contrast between summing welfare, which yields the repugnant conclusion, and averaging it, which avoids that conclusion but produces other counterintuitive results.

variants.name: The impossibility theorems
variants.text: Results associated with Gustaf Arrhenius arguing that no population axiology can satisfy all of a set of individually plausible adequacy conditions.

whyItMatters: The repugnant conclusion is a central problem of population ethics, forcing a reckoning with how to compare populations that differ in both the number and the quality of lives. It shows that the natural and widely held idea that betterness tracks total welfare leads to a conclusion almost everyone rejects, that a vast crowd of barely worthwhile lives can outrank a smaller flourishing world. This tension has generated decades of work seeking a consistent theory that avoids it, and the accompanying impossibility results suggest that every option carries some counterintuitive cost, a sobering lesson about the limits of population axiology. The problem bears directly on questions of enormous practical weight, from long-term policy and the ethics of future generations to debates within effective altruism about how much the sheer number of future people should matter.

working.text: adopt the view that a population's value is the sum of its members' well-being, so more positive lives always add to the total.
notice that enough barely worthwhile lives can outweigh fewer excellent ones on total welfare, yielding Z better than A.
seek a theory that avoids the conclusion, and confront that averaging brings new problems and impossibility results block a fully satisfactory fix.

limits: The repugnant conclusion is a problem for total utilitarianism in particular, and how damning it is depends on one's theory of population value; some philosophers bite the bullet and accept it, arguing the intuition of repugnance is unreliable when imagining astronomically large numbers. Alternatives that avoid it, such as average utilitarianism or critical-level views, incur their own counterintuitive consequences, and the impossibility theorems associated with Arrhenius suggest no theory escapes every plausible objection, though the precise formal conditions are technical and debated. The conclusion also involves idealised comparisons of enormous hypothetical populations, where intuitions may be shaky. So it functions as a deep constraint on population ethics that every theory must confront rather than a decisive refutation of any single view.
misreadings: The conclusion is not that a barely-worth-living life is worthless or bad; each such life is stipulated to be worth living, which is exactly why adding enough of them raises the total. It does not claim that quantity always trumps quality as a moral ideal, but that total-welfare reasoning implies it, which is why Parfit found the result repugnant rather than acceptable. And it is not cleanly avoided by any known theory: switching to averaging or other views trades one counterintuitive result for another, so presenting some particular fix as the settled escape misrepresents an unresolved problem.
origin: Identified by the philosopher Derek Parfit in his 1984 book Reasons and Persons, arising from total utilitarianism and the mere addition paradox in population ethics; Parfit sought but did not find a Theory X to avoid it, and later impossibility results deepen the difficulty.
